source: Wiemann et al. (2026) DiscoverPhysics, Appendix F Table 2 (capability gap per failed run)
finding: Every failed run on the 11 paper worlds was sorted by one main missing capability. The biggest single cause was never considering the right KIND of law (hidden species, time-varying coupling). That is a missing structure, not a bad parameter.
numbers: Failed runs: Opus 4.7 30 of 55 (45% pass), GPT-5.5 20 of 55 (64% pass). Considering the right kind of law: Opus 6, GPT-5.5 9 (15 of 50 failures, the top cause). Close-approach integrator: 2 and 8. Discriminating experiments: 8 and 1. Code not matching reasoning: 5 and 0. Real effect vs noise: 4 and 0. Acting on fitter signals: 2 and 2. When to stop: 3 and 0. Implicated in all four worlds where both models fail universally.
limits: Classification was done by an LLM (claude-opus-4-7, also a subject), one primary label per run, two passes. No per-world pass table in the text (heatmap only). Not a controlled structure-vs-parameter contrast.
agent_relevance: Best available number for frame-change failure: 30% of failures (15/50) are 'wrong kind of law'. Supports an explicit 'what kind of thing could be missing' step in O8.

source: Wiemann et al. (2026) DiscoverPhysics, Appendix F Table 3 (pipeline layer) and examples
finding: Failures were also sorted by pipeline layer. Self-monitoring (a contradiction was produced or received and not acted on) caused 8 of 30 Opus failures and 2 of 20 GPT-5.5 failures. The examples show the impasse signals that were ignored.
numbers: Layers (Opus/GPT-5.5): execution 8/8, reasoning 10/5, self-monitoring 8/2, prior knowledge 3/5, perception 1/0 (table text was garbled in extraction; row sums 30 and 20 match). Dark matter seed 3: Opus measured a 6.7-fold near-field acceleration excess and called it noise plus chaotic close encounters. three_species: Opus derived the per-particle structure and dropped it as overfitting; 4 consecutive GPT-5.5 fits plateaued at loss about 13 with no pivot. Opus submitted after 2 of 16 rounds on oscillator seed 0.
quote: no run hypothesises the ten hidden sources
limits: Same LLM-classifier caveat. Single seeds are anecdotes. Counts are small.
agent_relevance: Concrete S6 triggers seen in traces: a plateaued refit loss and a large unexplained residual excess. Both were ignored. Agent should log fit loss per round and treat 3+ flat refits as impasse.

source: Wiemann et al. (2026) DiscoverPhysics, guided vs random experiments and round budget (Section 4)
finding: Agent-chosen experiments beat random ones for the two best models. Opus improved monotonically with more rounds; GPT-5.5 stopped improving in pass rate and explanation after round 4 while MSE kept falling, i.e. more rounds refit parameters but did not change frame.
numbers: Round budgets 2, 4, 8, 16; five seeds per world, 22 worlds, 5,000 bootstrap resamples. GPT-5.5 ahead of Opus at 2, 4, 8 rounds; Opus ahead at 16. Best models pass about half the worlds. Token analysis not done for OpenAI models (hidden reasoning tokens).
limits: Numbers only in figures. No equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: More budget alone gives parameter refinement, not reframing. Supports an explicit reframe operator rather than 'think longer'.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) EvoSCM, Table 11 (extended ablation) read in full
finding: Each loop part was removed alone on DiscoverPhysics (GPT-5.5). Removing pre-committed prediction cost 11.6 points of explanation score, more than removing induction (8.7), deduction (8.0) or abduction (5.5). Only the SCM representation and the discriminative action cost more (about 27 points each).
numbers: Explanation score: full 75.09%; no SCM (free text) 48.18%; random action 47.45%; no pre-committed prediction 63.47% (norm MSE 4.79e-3 vs 2.77e-4); no induction 66.37%; no deduction 67.09%; no abduction 69.58%; free-form SCM rewrite 70.73%.
limits: One group, one benchmark. Ablations are not token-matched. Closes the 'each part separately' half of gap 2 for ablation, not for compute.
agent_relevance: Gives a ranking of what to keep: structured representation and discriminating experiments first, pre-commitment third. Pre-commitment is the cheapest to add (no extra experiments).

source: Zhao et al. (2026) EvoSCM, budget and token protocol (Appendix A.4, setup, Table 6)
finding: Episodes were matched, tokens were not. EvoSCM runs with the same world, seed, backbone, judge and round cap as the baseline, and its simulator-episode budget is capped at what the baseline used. Token use is shown only in a bar chart: more than baseline on DiscoverPhysics, fewer than GEPA, ReasoningBank and ModelSMC, fewer than baseline on the GRN benchmark.
numbers: Max 16 LLM rounds; population Kmax = 6. Population size: K=1 63.27% (norm MSE 6.78e-3), K=4 74.86%, K=6 75.09%, K=8 75.01%. Table 7 (GPT-5.6-Sol base): explanation 63.64% to 79.13%, episodes 5,296 to 3,543 (about one third fewer).
limits: No equal-token rerun exists. K=4 gets 98% of the K=6 score, so a small population is enough, but K cost in tokens is unreported. Gap 2 stays open for tokens.
agent_relevance: A population of about 4 competing models is the cheap setting. Part of the gain (K=1 to K=4, 11.6 points) is population; the rest comes from the structured form.

source: Huang et al. (2026) DISCERN: Can AI Agents Work Like Scientists and Guide Discovery? (arXiv 2609.33357)
finding: Benchmark where Level 3 asks for hypotheses and revision under adversarial review. In counterfactual dossiers the agent's own prior is elicited BEFORE the evidence, and the dossier counts only if the evidence conflicts with that prior. That is a pre-registered-expectation anomaly test with an LLM.
numbers: 203 tasks, 8 life-science tracks, 8 models. Perfect scores: 60.8% of L1, 34.2% of L2, 0.6% of L3 evaluations. L3: 22 dossiers = 8 real controls (evidence agrees with prior), 6 native counterfactuals, 8 injected counterfactuals. 94 hypotheses submitted; 46.8% got no novelty credit, 30.9% got at least two thirds.
limits: Life-science data analysis, not physics frames. Revision is scored by rubric and LLM review, not as frame change. Controls include a fake-anomaly check (scRNA CD4 case: flagging an anomaly is 'over-diagnosis').
agent_relevance: Closest published test of artefact versus real anomaly with an LLM. Shows the control-case design we need: some surprises are fake.

source: Huang et al. (2026) DISCERN, caution and commitment results (Section 4.3, Figure 4, Appendix A.3)
finding: Models split into two failure styles when evidence conflicts with their stated prior: commit (Kimi) or abstain on everything (Astra). Neither is calibrated. On clean controls most models wrongly rejected sound data. Rankings on evidence judgement are unstable across tracks.
numbers: Kimi submitted a hypothesis in 92.3% of eligible counterfactual cases; Astra abstained in 100%. Only 19 of 64 L1 clean-control evaluations (29.7%) correctly accepted the sound data; Astra 12.5%, Opus 62.5%. Sol and Opus: conditional novelty 41.7 vs 41.2, but they submitted on 18.2% vs 81.0% of eligible tasks. Concessions to reviewers: DeepSeek 41.7% of outcomes, Opus 5.9%. Kendall W across tracks: L3 commitment 0.45, evidence fidelity 0.27, return to prior 0.22, clean specificity 0.15.
limits: Eligible counts small. W is low partly from ties.
agent_relevance: Gives both error rates for gap 4: false rejection of sound data (about 70% of clean controls) and refusal to commit on a real conflict. A hold-then-replicate rule must be tested against both.

source: Huang et al. (2026) DISCERN, revision quality example (DUSP4 case, Appendix H)
finding: Conceding more is not revising better. DeepSeek conceded most often but also gave the best revision here: it narrowed its mechanistic claim and proposed an experiment that would separate the two chromatin signals.
numbers: Task score 95.7 for the narrowed claim with a discriminating test. Three rounds of adversarial review per committed hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Reframe should end in a narrower claim plus a test that separates it from the old frame, not in a flip.

source: Hudson (2001) Discoveries, when and by whom? Br. J. Philos. Sci. 52(1):75-91, as presented in Schindler (2024) Kuhn on Scientific Discovery
finding: Philosophers dispute Kuhn's oxygen account. Hudson says Priestley discovered oxygen because he had a base description that picked it out (a respirable, combustible constituent of air shown by the nitrous-air test), even though his theory was wrong. Kuhn says discovery needs the right conceptualisation and took time. Schindler keeps Kuhn's extended-process point but accepts Hudson's correctness problem.
numbers: Kuhn: three stages (awareness of anomaly, exploration, adjustment). Priestley 1774: thought it nitrous oxide, 1775: dephlogisticated air. Lavoisier 1775: 'good common air'. Scheele unpublished in time (Hudson 2001 disputes the weight of this). X-rays 1895: found by accident with no clash with a held theory, needed change in instrument expectations.
limits: Secondary source (a 2024 philosophy chapter). Primary lab notebooks and Priestley/Lavoisier texts not opened.
agent_relevance: Not every discovery starts with an anomaly (X-rays by accident, Priestley by experiment). Treat 'anomaly first' as one entry route, and keep a route for accidental findings.

source: Schindler (2024) Kuhn on Scientific Discovery, on when anomalies lead to change, with Bruner and Postman as retold
finding: Kuhn's answer to why anomalies are noticed at all: only against a very strong sense of what is normal. Resistance to change is useful because only anomalies that reach the core of knowledge then force change. Whether a given anomaly is bracketed or forces change cannot be decided in advance.
numbers: Bruner and Postman (1949) as retold: threshold for correct identification four times higher for anomalous than normal cards (114 ms vs 28 ms); cards shown 3 times, exposure from 10 ms rising until two correct identifications or 1 s; 10% of subjects still failed at 1 s.
quote: the anomalies that lead to paradigm change will penetrate existing knowledge to the core
limits: Second-hand again. Bruner and Postman numbers not read from the 1949 paper (DOI 10.1111/j.1467-6494.1949.tb01241.x, 389 citations per Crossref).
agent_relevance: Supports a high bar to drop a frame: tie the trigger to anomalies that are large, repeated or near the core claim.

source: Trickett, Trafton, Schunn and Harrison (2001) That's odd! How scientists respond to anomalous data (Cogsci 2001), full text
finding: Extension of Dunbar's in vivo method to data analysis in two fields. Scientists noticed anomalies and attended more to them than to expected phenomena, usually by proposing a hypothesis and elaborating it from the visual display rather than from theory.
numbers: 3 scientists in 2 domains: 2 astronomers (ring galaxy data, about 53 min, 649 on-task segments, 19 episodes) and 1 physicist (about 15 min, 176 segments, 9 episodes). Later references to anomalies vs expected: astronomy 7.6 vs 1.5, physics 3.0 vs 1.25.
limits: N = 3, single sessions. Not an independent replication; same group extending its own method.
agent_relevance: No replication with computational scientists was found. Treat 'experts attend to surprise' as small-sample evidence.

source: Alberdi, Sleeman and Korpi (2000) Accommodating surprise in taxonomic tasks: the role of expertise. Cognitive Science 24(1):53-91
finding: Independent field and task (plant taxonomy, rogue item) supports the idea that experts attend to anomalies and that domain knowledge drives how they revise. Participants searched domain knowledge for a new hypothesis that would accommodate the surprise.
numbers: 5 professional botanists, think-aloud, category defined by an unusual feature; strategies combined into a model of knowledge-guided inductive categorisation.
limits: Only the Crossref abstract and the Trickett et al. description were read; the publisher full text returned 403. N = 5.
agent_relevance: Second field with the same direction of effect, but tiny N. Gap 6 only partly closed.

source: Chinn and Brewer (1998) An empirical test of a taxonomy of responses to anomalous data in science. J. Res. Sci. Teach. 35(6):623-654 (ERIC EJ570943 record)
finding: Only the catalogue record could be opened. It says the study tested a taxonomy of seven proposed responses and concluded that one additional type was needed. That fits the eight-type count in earlier notes. No sample sizes or frequencies are in the record.
numbers: 7 proposed response types tested; 1 added = 8. 57 references. No N, no frequencies, no factor effects obtained.
limits: Abstract-level only. The 4/32 and 6/10 figures remain unverified. Wiley full text returned 403.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open. Do not cite any frequency from this paper in the schema until the PDF is read.

source: Brewer and Chinn (1994) Scientists' responses to anomalous data: evidence from psychology, history, and philosophy of science. PSA 1994 vol 1:304-313 (Cambridge page)
finding: Page confirms the paper's aim: a systematic account of the role of anomaly in theory change, with a naturalist approach and evidence from history and psychology of science.
agent_relevance: Citation check only; no new numbers.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the capabilities and limitations of language models through counterfactual tasks (NAACL; arXiv 2307.02477)
finding: Closest measured LLM analogue to Bruner and Postman normalisation: 11 tasks where the familiar default condition is altered (base-9 arithmetic, 1-based indexing, rotated axes). GPT-4 does well on the default and substantially worse on the altered version, which points to reliance on the familiar template.
numbers: 11 tasks; GPT-4 with 0-shot chain of thought underperforms on every counterfactual variant. Few-shot CoT with up to 16 examples narrows the gap but it stays substantial for bases 9, 11 and 16. Exact accuracies are in figures and were not extracted.
limits: The altered rule is stated in the prompt, so this tests following a changed rule, not noticing a hidden anomaly. Models predate the 2026 frontier.
agent_relevance: Evidence that familiar templates dominate even when the change is stated. Gap 10 only partly closed: no study found that tests unannounced contradictory items, or a prompt that removes it.

finding: No study found that compares impasse triggers (residual threshold vs failure count vs prediction-error log), tests a forced 'name an alternative frame first' step against false reframes, or checks how many Bayesian-surprise hypotheses are already implied by logged results. arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate limited and the shared WebSearch budget ran out after 3 queries, so this is a thin negative.
numbers: 3 WebSearch calls returned Chinn/Brewer pages, DISCERN, HypoArena, DiscoverPhysics and SciPost LHC-anomaly agents. None addresses the four gaps directly.
limits: Absence of evidence under limited search. Retry when API limits reset.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 8, 9 must be settled by our own ablation, not by citation.

source: Before the Action: Benchmarking LLMs on Prospective Hypothesis Discovery (HypoArena), arXiv 2607.15766 (page summary)
finding: 988 cases in 6 domains where context holds anomalous observations and 'unresolved tensions'; models must build grounded, testable hypothesis sets. Anomalies are inputs, not a separate analysis; no abandon-or-reframe measurement.
numbers: Arena rating (BTD): claude-sonnet-4.6 1654.0 (71.3% win), claude-opus-4.6 1652.7, gpt-5.4 1631.4, gemini-3.1-pro 1394.0. Agent-mode structured skills shift ratings from +88 to about -58, Spearman with baseline -0.10. Some traces show candidate compression (several lines reasoned, narrower set submitted). Rubric scores 95-98% at or above 4.0 (ceiling).
limits: Read via a fetch summary, not the PDF. LLM-judged. Not about frames the model already holds.
agent_relevance: A structured-skill prompt can hurt strong models (about -58 for Opus 4.6), a warning for adding a forced alternative-frame step without testing it.
